question:
1. With reference to soil conservation, consider the following practices: [UPSC CSE Pre 2010]
  2. Crop rotation
  3. Sand fences 3. Terracing
  4. Windbreaks Which of the above are considered appropriate methods for soil conservation in India?
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer All of the methods mentioned are appropriate methods for soil conservation in India.

  • Crop rotation is a method of planting different crops in the same field in a planned sequence. This helps to prevent soil depletion and improve soil fertility.
  • Sand fences are barriers made of sand, straw, or other materials that are used to trap wind-blown sand. They are used to prevent desertification and to protect crops and land from wind erosion.
  • Terracing is a method of farming that involves building steps on the side of a hill. This helps to level the land and prevent the soil from eroding.
  • Windbreaks are rows of trees or shrubs that are planted to protect crops and land from wind erosion.

Important Tips

Other methods for soil conservation in India:

  • Contour farming: Plowing and planting crops along the contours of the land to help slow down the flow of water.
  • Strip cropping: Planting different crops in strips next to each other to help break up the wind and water.
  • Mulching: Covering the soil with organic material, such as straw or leaves, to help protect the soil from the wind and water.
  • Afforestation: Planting trees and shrubs to help hold the soil in place.

Exp) Option a is the correct answer. The Nilgiri Mountains form part of the Western Ghats in northwestern Tamil Nadu, Southern Karnataka, and eastern Kerala in India. They are known for their scenic beauty and are home to several national parks, including Mudumalai, Mukurthi, and Silent Valley. question: 1. From north towards south, which one of the following is the correct sequence of the given rivers in India? [UPSC CSE Pre 2006]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. The correct sequence of the rivers from north to south is Shyok - Zaskar - Spiti - Satluj. [Image: Map showing the river sequence]

Important Tips

Shyok River:

  • Rising from the Karakoram Range, it flows through the Northern Ladakh region in J&K.
  • It has a length of about 550km.
  • A tributary of the Indus River, it originates from the Rimo Glacier. The river widens at the confluence with the Nubra River.
  • Shyok River marks the south-eastern fringe of the Karakoram ranges by forming a V-shaped bend around it.

Spiti River:

  • Spiti river is a 225 kilometres (140 mi) long tributary of Sutlej River.
  • The Spiti River nurtures the beautiful valleys of Lahaul-Spiti district of Himachal Pradesh.
  • It originates from the Kunzum Range of the Himalayas in a way that divides Lahaul and Spiti.

Zanskar River:

  • The Zanskar River is the first major tributary of the Indus River, equal or greater in volume than the main river, which flows entirely within Ladakh.
  • It originates northeast of the Great Himalayan range and drains both the Himalayas and the Zanskar Range within the region of Zanskar.
  • It flows northeast to join the Indus River near Nimo.

question: 1. Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the given Indian cities in the decreasing order of their normal annual rainfall? [UPSC CSE Pre 2005]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. The correct sequence of the given Indian cities in the decreasing order of their normal annual rainfall is Kochi (3228.3 mm) - Kolkata (1,582 mm) - Patna (1000 -1237 mm) - Delhi (707 mm).

  • Kochi: Kochi has a tropical wet and dry climate, which means it has hot and humid summers and mild winters. The average annual temperature is 27.3 °C, and the average annual rainfall is 3228.3 mm. Kochi receives most of its rainfall from the southwest monsoon, which lasts from June to September.
  • Kolkata: Kolkata also has a tropical wet and dry climate, but it is slightly cooler and drier than Kochi. The average annual temperature is 26.8 °C, and the average annual rainfall is 1582 mm. Kolkata receives rainfall from both the southwest and northeast monsoons, which occur from June to September and from October to December respectively.
  • Patna: Patna has a humid subtropical climate, which means it has hot summers and cool winters. The average annual temperature is 26.4 °C, and the average annual rainfall is 1116 mm. Patna receives rainfall from both the southwest and northeast monsoons, which occur from June to September and from October to December respectively.
  • Delhi: Delhi has a semi-arid climate, which means it has very hot summers and cold winters. The average annual temperature is 25.1 °C, and the average annual rainfall is 707 mm. Delhi receives most of its rainfall from the southwest monsoon, which lasts from July to September.

  2. Silent Valley National Park is in the Nallamalla range.
  3. Pathrakkadavu Hydroelectric project is proposed to be built near the Silent Valley National Park.
  4. The Kunthi river originates in Silent Valley's rainforests.
    Which of the statements given above is/are correct? [UPSC CSE Pre 2005]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. Statement 1 is incorrect: Silent Valley National Park, situated in Kerala’s Nilgiri hills, spans 89.52 km2. It lies at the border of Mannarkkad Taluk in Palakkad district, Nilambur Taluk in Malappuram district, Kerala, and Nilgiris district, Tamil Nadu. Whereas Nallamalla Range are a section of the Eastern Ghats which forms the eastern boundary of Rayalaseema region of the state of Andhra Pradesh and Nagarkurnool district of the state of Telangana, in India. Statement 2 is correct: The Pathrakkadavu Hydroelectric project (PHEP) is proposed near the Silent Valley National Park in Palakkad district, Kerala. The project, sanctioned in 2007, aims to build a 64.5-meter-high dam on the Kunthi river, with a storage capacity of 0.872 million cubic meters, to generate 70 MW of power. Statement 3 is correct: The Kunthi river is a waterway located in the state of Kerala, India. It flows through the Silent Valley National Park. This river is also called as Thuthapuzha by thelocal population. Kunthi river-is-one-of the main tributaries of the Bharathapuzha River, the second longest river in Kerala.

Important Tips

Additional Facts on Silent Valley National Park:

  • Lion tailed macaques is the flagship species of the Park.
  • The indigenous tribal groups that live within park boundaries include Irulas, Kurumbas, Mudugas and Kattunaikkars, the ethnic heritage of these communities is well protected.
  • Karimpuzha Wildlife Sanctuary, New Amarambalam Reserved Forest, and Nedumkayam Rainforest in Nilambur Taluk of Malappuram district, Attappadi Reserved Forest in Mannarkkad Taluk of Palakkad district, and Mukurthi National Park of Nilgiris district, are located around Silent Valley National Park.

Code: [UPSC CSE Pre 2002]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer. The mangroves and their locations:

  • Achra Ratnagiri mangroves are found in Maharashtra
  • Coondapur mangroves are found in Karnataka
  • Pichavaram mangroves are found in Tamil Nadu
  • Vembanad mangroves are found in Kerala

Important Tips

Mangroves:

  • Mangroves are a unique type of coastal ecosystem found in tropical and subtropical regions. They are dense forests of salt-tolerant trees and shrubs that thrive in intertidal zones, where land meets the sea.
  • Mangroves exhibit Viviparity mode of reproduction, where seeds germinate within the tree before falling to the ground.
  • Mangrove plants have special roots like prop roots and pneumatophores, which help impede water flow and provide support in the challenging tidal environment.
  • According to the Indian State Forest Report 2021, Mangrove cover in India is 4992 sq. Km which is 0.15% of the country’s total geographical area.
  • Sunderban in West Bengal is the largest mangrove forest region in the world.
  • West Bengal has approximately 40% of India’s mangrove forests.
  • The second largest mangrove forest in India is Bhitarkanika in Odisha created by the two river deltas of River Brahmani and Baitarani.
  • Top states/UTs having maximum mangrove forest area are - West Bengal, Gujarat, A&N Islands, Andhra Pradesh

question: 1. Identify the correct order of the process of soil-erosion form the following: [UPSC CSE Pre 2001]
options: Splash erosion, Sheet erosion, Rill erosion, Gully erosion
Sheet erosion, Splash erosion, Gully erosion, Rill erosion
Rill erosion, Gully erosion, Sheet erosion, Splash erosion
Gully erosion, Rill erosion, Sheet erosion, Splash erosion
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer The correct order of the process of soil erosion is: Splash erosion --> Sheet erosion --> Rill erosion --> Gully erosion.

  • Splash erosion is the smallest and most initial form of soil erosion. It occurs when raindrops hit the soil surface and dislodge small particles of soil. These particles are then carried away by wind or water.
  • Sheet erosion is a more advanced form of soil erosion. It occurs when the top layer of soil is removed by water or wind. Sheet erosion can be preventedby planting cover crops and using conservation practices, such as contour farming.
  • Rill erosion is a more serious form of soil erosion. It occurs when small channels are formed in the soil by water runoff. Rill erosion can be preventedby using conservation practices, such as terracing and strip cropping.
  • Gully erosion is the most serious form of soil erosion. It occurs when large channels are formed in the soil by water runoff. Gully erosion can be very difficult to control and can lead to the complete loss of soil.
    Page 194

Important Tips

Ghaghara River:

  • The Ghaghara River, alternatively known as Karnali or Kauriala, originates from the glaciers of Mapchachungo on the Tibetan plateau near Lake Mansarovar.
  • It traverses through the Himalayas in Nepal and enters India, where it is joined by the Sharda River at Brahmaghat.
  • The Ghaghara is a major left-bank tributary of the Ganga River and eventually joins it at Chhapra in Bihar.
  • The total length of the Ghaghara River is approximately 1080 kilometers.
  • It serves as the primary source of water for the Bara-Banki District of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Key tributaries of the Ghaghara include Rapti, Chhoti Gandak, Sharda, and Sarju.

Kosi River:

  • Also known as Saptakoshi, the Kosi River is an antecedent transboundary river that flows through Nepal and India.
  • Several of its tributaries, such as the Arun, Sun Kosi, and Bhote Koshi, originate in Tibet.
  • This 729-kilometer-long river is one of the largest tributaries of the Ganga and joins it at Kursela in Kathiar district.
  • Mt. Everest and Kanchenjunga, the world’s highest peaks, are situated in the Kosi catchment area.
  • Bagmati is a significant tributary.
  • The Kosi River has shifted its course more than 120 kilometers from east to west in the last 250 years, earning it the nickname “The Sorrow of Bihar” due to its unstable nature and heavy monsoon silt.

Gandak River:

  • It is formed by the union of the Kali and Trisuli rivers, which rise in the Great Himalayan Range in Nepal. From this junction to the Indian border the river is called the Narayani.
  • It enters the Ganga River opposite Patna in a place called Sonepur after a winding course of 765 km.
  • The Burhi Gandak flows parallel to and east of the Gandak River.
  • The upper catchment area of the river is bleak and desolate, lying in the rain shadow area of the Himalayan range.

question: 1. The Himalayas are formed of parallel fold ranges, of which the oldest range is- [UPSC CSE Pre 1994]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. The oldest range in the Himalayas is the Great Himalayan Range. Its formation resulted from the collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, around 50 million years ago. This collision led to the uplift of sedimentary rocks and the creation of parallel fold ranges. Various geological mechanisms, such as subduction, extrusion, and thrusting, played roles in shaping the Himalayas, ultimately resulting in the impressive topographic relief we see today.

Important Tips

Chronology of Formation of Himalayan Ranges:

  • The Great Himalayan Range is the oldest among the Himalayan ranges. It began forming around 50 million years ago when the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. This collision resulted in the initial uplift of sediments and the formation of the Great Himalayan Range.
  • Following the initial collision, the Lesser Himalayas began to form as a result of continued tectonic pressure and the folding of sediments. This process started shortly after the Great Himalayan Range began to rise, roughly 20 to 50 million years ago.
  • The Dhauladhar Range is a subrange of the Lesser Himalayas. It formed concurrently with the Lesser Himalayas, approximately 20 to 50 million years ago, as a result of the same tectonic forces and geological processes.
  • The Shiwalik Range is the youngest of the Himalayan ranges. It began forming relatively more recently, around 2 to 20 million years ago, due to the ongoing collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates. This range primarily consists of unconsolidated sediments and foothills.

question: 1. Farmland tends to erode most rapidly when planted with: [UPSC CSE Pre 1994]
explanation:

Statement 1 is correct:Sorghum is a tall, grassy plant that is grown for its grain and forage. It is a deep-rooted crop, which means that it can tap into deep layers of soil for water and nutrients. However, sorghum is also a thirsty crop, which means that it can deplete the soil of moisture. When sorghum is planted continuously in the same field, the soil can become depleted of moisture and nutrients. This makes the soil more susceptible to erosion, especially by wind. Statement 2, 3, and 4 are incorrect: Potato, wheat, and clover are not as susceptible to erosion as sorghum. Potato is a shallow-rooted crop, which means that it does not tap into deep layers of soil for water and nutrients. Wheat is a moderate-rooted crop, clover is a shallow-rooted crop that also fixes nitrogen in the soil.

Important Tips

Other crops that are susceptible to erosion:

  • Cotton: Cotton plants have relatively shallow root systems, and their fields are often tilled between planting seasons, leaving the soil vulnerable to erosion.
  • Sugarcane: Sugarcane is grown in tropical regions and often on slopes. The steep terrain and shallow root system can make it prone to soil erosion.
  • Vegetable Crops: Some vegetable crops, like lettuce and carrots, have shallow roots and may be planted in rows with exposed soil in between.
  • Orchards and Vineyards: Young orchards and vineyards may have limited ground cover and shallow roots, increasing the risk of erosion.

1. Given below are two Statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
    Assertion (A): The Himalayas are still rising.
    Reason (R): The Indian tectonic plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate.
    Select the correct answer from the codes given below: [UPPCS (Pre) 2024]
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. Statement A is correct. The Himalayas, which are the youngest fold mountain ranges in the world, are geologically active and still growing in height. Modern geodetic and satellite data (such as GPS measurements) confirm that many parts of the Himalayas are rising by a few millimeters to centimeters each year. This phenomenon occurs due to the ongoing tectonic activity in the region. Statement R is correct and explains statement A. The Himalayas were formed as a result of the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate that began around 50 million years ago. This convergent plate boundary continues to be active today, with the Indian plate pushing northward into the Eurasian plate at a rate of about 5 cm per year. As a result of this compression, the crust is forced upward, leading to the uplift and growth of the Himalayas.

Important Tips

Himalayas

  1. Young Fold Mountains: The Himalayas are the youngest and highest fold mountain range in the world, formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.
  2. Geological Age: Formed around 50 million years ago during the Tertiary period.
  3. Extent: Stretch across five countries—India, Nepal, Bhutan, China, and Pakistan—covering about 2,400 km from Indus in the west to Brahmaputra in the east.
  4. Three Parallel Ranges:
  • Himadri (Greater Himalayas) - Highest, includes Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga.
  • Himachal (Lesser Himalayas) – Includes hill stations like Shimla and Mussoorie.
  • Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas) - Lowest, made of unconsolidated sediments.
  1. Source of Rivers: Origin of major rivers like Ganga, Indus, and Brahmaputra.
    Page 200

question:
1. With reference to the Himalayan range, which of the statements is/are correct?
  2. The sedimentary rocks of the greater Himalayas were fossil less. 2. Marine livings fossils are found in the sedimentary rocks of lesser Himalayas.
  3. Remains of human civilization are found in the outer or Shivalik Himalayas.
    Select the correct answer using the codes given below: [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2019]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. Statement 1 is incorrect: The sedimentary rocks of the greater Himalayas are not fossil less. While these rocks have undergone significant metamorphism due to the intense geological processes associated with mountain building, they were originally formed in ancient marine environments. As a result, they can contain fossils, although fossils found in these rocks may be relatively rare and poorly preserved compared to thosein less metamorphosed sedimentary rocks. On a few peaks, such as Mount Everest, the crystalline rocks carried old fossil-bearing Tethys sediments from the north piggyback to the summits. Statement 2 is correct: The sedimentary rocks of the lesser Himalayas do indeed contain marine fossils. These rocks were once part of ancient marine environments and have preserved fossils of marine organisms. While fossils may not be as abundant or diverse as those in the Tethyan Himalayas, they are still found in sedimentary rocks of the lesser Himalayas. Statement 3 is correct: It is true that remains of ancient human civilizations have been found in the outer or Shivalik Himalayas. These areas have been important archaeological sites, yielding tools, artifacts, and fossils that provide insights into early human habitation in the region.

question: 1. In which of the following rivers, the upper course contains freshwater but saline water flowing at the lower part? [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2019]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. The Luni River in northwest India exhibits the characteristic of having freshwater in its upper course but becoming saline as it flows towards the lower part. The upper course of the Luni River has freshwater primarily because it receives its water from relatively fresh sources such as rainfall, seasonal streams, and rivers originating in the Aravalli Range. During the monsoon season, these sources contribute freshwater to the river, giving it its initial freshwater character in the upper reaches. However, as the river flows through the arid Thar Desert with high evaporation rates and encounters naturally occurring salts in the soil and rocks, the water gradually becomes more saline in its lower course.

Important Tips

Additional facts on Luni River

  • The Luni or the Salt River (Lonari or Lavanavari in Sanskrit) is named so because its water is brackish below Balotra.
  • Luni is the only river basin of any significance in Western Rajasthan, which forms the bulk of the arid zone.
  • Luni originates from the western slopesof the Aravalli ranges at an elevation of 772 m near Ajmer flowing in the southwest direction and traversing a course of 511 km in Rajasthan, it finally flows into the Rann of Kachchh (it gets lost in the marsh).
  • Most of its tributaries drain the steep northwest of Aravalli hills and join it on the left side. Its total catchment area falls in Rajasthan.

question: 1. Kuttanad (or Kuttanadu) of Kerala is famous for: [U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2015]
options: The region with the lowest altitude in India
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. Kuttanad, also known as Kuttanadu, in Kerala is famous for being the region with the lowest altitude in India, situated at 2.2 meters below sea level. It is renowned as the “Rice Bowl of Kerala” due to extensive rice farming practices in the area. Kuttanad is unique as it is one of the few places globally where farming is conducted below sea level. Kuttanad farmers are noted for Biosaline Farming (growth of plants in saline groundwater or soil). In 2013, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) declared this farming style as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System (GIAHS). It is also famous for Vallamkali boat race in the Punnamada Backwaters.

Important Tips

Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS):
GIAHS are distinctive land use systems worldwide, characterized by rich biodiversity, resilient ecosystems, and cultural heritage. These systems are managed by local communities, including farmers, herders, fisherfolk, and tribals. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (UN FAO) leads the GIAHS program.

  • Pampore Saffron Heritage, Jammu & Kashmir (2011):
  • Known for saffron cultivation, which is integral to Kashmiri cuisine, medicinal traditions, and cultural heritage.

  • Koraput Traditional Agriculture, Odisha (2012):
  • Located in the Eastern Ghats, this region practices subsistence paddy cultivation on highland slopes.
  • Strong ties with tribal communities, sacred groves for plant genetic resource preservation.
  • Kuttanad Below Sea Level Farming System, Kerala (2013):
  • It comprises wetlands for paddy cultivation and fishing, garden lands for coconut and food crops, and water areas for inland fishing.
  • Rice cultivation below sea level in land created by draining delta swamps in brackish waters.

    Assertion (A): The rivers of Western Ghats do not form the delta.
    Reason (R): They flow through short courses with high speed over hard rocks.
    Select the correct answer from the codes given below: [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2014]
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer. Assertion (A): It is true that the rivers of the Western Ghats do not form deltas. Deltas are typically formed along the eastern coast of India. Reason (R) is true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A): Rivers in the Western Ghats region typically do not form deltas. This is because they have shorter courses and flow over hard rocks, which limits the deposition of sediments necessary for delta formation. Deltas are more commonly associated with rivers that have longer courses and flow over softer sedimentary terrain.

Important Tips

West flowing rivers of peninsular India don't form deltas because of following reasons:

  • Short Course: Many of the rivers in the Western Ghats region have relatively short courses before they reach the Arabian Sea. These shorter courses do not allow for the extensive deposition of sediments that are necessary for delta formation.
  • Hard Rocks: The Western Ghats are characterized by hard rocks, including basaltic formations. These rocks do not erode easily and do not contribute significant amounts of sediment to the rivers.
  • High Gradient: The Western Ghats have a steep gradient, which means that the rivers flow rapidly. Fast-flowing rivers have less time to deposit sediment, which is essential for delta formation.
  • Lack of Alluvial Plains: Unlike the rivers originating in the Himalayas, which have vast alluvial plains, the Western Ghats rivers do not have extensive low-lying areas where sediment can accumulate to form deltas.
  • Direct Entry into the Sea: Instead of forming deltas, many Western Ghats rivers enter the Arabian Sea directly. They do not meander and deposit sediments in the way that rivers with longer courses and lower gradients do.
    Page 208

question: 1. Which of the following rivers is an example of the superimposed river? [U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2007]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. Chambal Riveris an example of the superimposed river. Superimposed drainage, also known as epigenetic or superinduced drainage, occurs when a river maintains its course and pattern on a landscape that has undergone significant changes due to geological processes. In this type of drainage, the river's current path doesnt align with the underlying rock structure or geological features because it was established on a previous layer of rocks that have since eroded away. The river retains its original course unaffected by the newly exposed geological features. Examples of superimposed rivers include the Damodar, Subarnarekha, Chambal, Banas, and several rivers in the Rewa Plateau. These rivers flow independently of the current topography, following their initial paths set before significant geological changes occurred. The Alaknanda River, Kosi River, and Godavari River all flow through regions with a single geological history. Their drainage patterns are consistent with the underlying rock structure.

Important Tips

Discordant drainage patterns:
Discordant drainage patterns are characterized by rivers that do not align with the surrounding topography and geology. They are classified into two main types: antecedent and superimposed.

  • Antecedent Drainage (Inconsequent Drainage):
  • Occurs when a part of the river slope and the surrounding area undergo uplift.
  • The river maintains its original course, cutting through the uplifted portion.
  • This cutting action results in the formation of deep gorges.
  • It is characterized by vertical erosion or vertical downcutting.
  • Antecedent rivers are typically older than the geological features they traverse.
  • Examples include the Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra rivers, which are older than the Himalayan Mountain range.
    Page 211

question: 1. The paleomagnetic results obtained from India indicate that in the past, the Indian land mass has moved: [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 1998]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer. The paleomagnetic results obtained from India indicate that in the past, the Indian landmass has moved northward. This is because the magnetic field of the Earth has reversed its polarity several times in the past, and the rocks in India record these reversals. By studying the orientation of the magnetic minerals in these rocks, scientists can determine the direction in which the Indian landmass was moving at the time the rocks were formed. The Indian landmass was once part of the Gondwana supercontinent, which also included Africa, South America, Australia, and Antarctica. About 180 million years ago, Gondwana began to break apart, and the Indian landmass began to drift northward. It collided with the Eurasian landmass about 40 million years ago, and this collision caused the formation of the Himalayas. The northward movement of the Indian landmass is still ongoing, and it is estimated that Indian landmass is moving about 5 centimeters per year. This slow movement is causing the Himalayas to rise at a rate of about 1 centimeter per year.

Important Tips

Paleomagnetism:

  • Paleomagnetism is a field of study that investigates the Earth’s magnetic field history using records found in rocks, sediments, and archaeological materials.
  • Paleomagnetism helps detect the polarity of the Earth’s magnetic field and identifies magnetic field reversals over time. This is possible by studying rocks of different ages.
  • Basaltic rocks, which make up a significant portion of the ocean floor, contain magnetic minerals. As these rocks solidify, these minerals align with the prevailing magnetic field, preserving its direction.
  • Paleomagnetic studies have shown that the orientation of the Earth’s magnetic field has alternated over geological time, a phenomenon known as geomagnetic reversal.
  • Paleomagnetism played a crucial role in supporting the continental drift hypothesis and the development of theories like Sea Floor Spreading and Plate Tectonics.
    Page 213, 214

explanation:

Statement 1 is correct: Devprayag is a town in Uttarakhand, India, where the Alaknanda and Bhagirathi rivers converge to form the Ganges River, known as the Ganga. This confluence is one of the Panch Prayag (five confluences) along the Ganges’s course. The meeting point of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers, where they converge to form the Ganges River (Ganga), is Devprayag. Located near New Tehri city in Tehri Garhwal District in Uttarakhand, Devprayag is one of the five sacred confluences known as the Panch Prayag. Statement 2 is correct: Rudraprayag, situated in Uttarakhand, India, is where the Mandakini and Alaknanda rivers converge to form the Alaknanda River. Statement 3 is correct: The Alaknanda originates from Badrinath in Uttarakhand and is one of the two primary tributaries of the Ganges, along with the Bhagirathi. Together, they form the sacred Ganges River in Northern India. Statement 4 is incorrect: Shankaracharya was an early 8th century Indian philosopher and theologian who consolidated the doctrine of Advaita Vedanta. He established four major mathas in different regions of India - Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, and Sringeri. These mathas were founded to promote Advaita Vedanta and Sanatana Dharma. question:
1. Compare the Himalayan Rivers with the Peninsular Rivers based on the following comparisons:
  2. Most of the Himalayan rivers are perennial, whereas most ofthe Peninsular rivers are rain fed.
  3. The gradient of the Himalayan River is steeper than the Peninsular River.
  4. The Peninsular River causes more erosion on its way in comparison to the Himalayan River.
    Choose the correct answer from the options given below. [67th BPSC (Pre) 2022]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer. Statement 1 is correct: Most of the rivers originating from the Himalayas are perennial, meaning they flow throughout the year. This is because they are primarily fed by snowmelt from the Himalayan glaciers and receive consistent water supply from the melting snow even during dry seasons. In contrast, many peninsular rivers are rain-fed, which means their flow is highly dependent on seasonal rainfall. During the monsoon season, these rivers can swell significantly, but they may experience reduced flow or even dry up during the dry season when there is less rainfall. Statement 2 is correct: The Himalayan rivers have steeper gradients or slopes because they originate from the high mountain ranges of the Himalayas. The rapid descent from the mountains results in fast-flowing and turbulent rivers. Whereas peninsular rivers generally have gentler gradients as they flow through the relatively flat Deccan Plateau. They tend to have slower and less turbulent flows compared to the Himalayan rivers. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Himalayan River, with its steep gradients and powerful flow, causes more erosion compared to Peninsular Rivers. This is due to the rugged terrain it traverses, carrying large amounts of sediment eroded from the mountains. In contrast, Peninsular Rivers flow over relatively stable landforms, resulting in lower erosion rates and sediment transport.

Important Tips

The difference between Himalayan and Peninsular Rivers:

Himalayan Rivers Peninsular Rivers
These rivers originate from the Himalayan Mountain ranges. These rivers originate from the peninsular plateaus.
They are longer and larger than the peninsular rivers. They are comparatively smaller than the Himalayan Rivers.
They have larger basins and catchment areas. They have smaller basins and catchment areas.
The bedrocks of these rivers are soft, sedimentary and easily erodible. The bedrocks of these rivers are hard and not easily erodible.
They are perennial in nature. They are seasonal and non-perennial.
They are fed by the meltwater from glaciers/ rains. They are fed only by rain.
They form V-shaped valleys. They form U-shaped valleys.
They form meanders. They may not form meanders.
They form big deltas. They form estuaries.
They are antecedent rivers. They are consequent rivers.

Additional facts on Kanwar Lake:

question: 1. Rajasthan receives very little rain because: [67th BPSC (Pre) (Re-Exam) 2022]
options: the monsoon fails to reach this area
there is no water available and thus the winds remain dry
the winds do not come across any barriers to cause the necessary uplift to cool the air
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer. Rajasthan receives very little rain because of its geographical location and the orientation of the Aravalli range. The Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon that causes rains in western and south-western India runs parallel to the Aravalli range and thus hardly causes any rainfall as the winds do not get interrupted (winds do not come across any barriers to cause the necessary uplift to cool the air). The Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon also fails to reach Rajasthan as it is blocked by the Himalayas and the Vindhya range. Therefore, the winds that reach Rajasthan are dry and hot and do not bring any moisture.

question:
1. Consider the following statements regarding formation of landforms in India:
  2. Structurally, the Meghalaya plateau is an extended part of the Deccan plateau. 2. The Valley of Kashmir was formed in a synclinorium.
  3. The Gangetic plain was formed in a fore deep. 4. The Himalayas originated as a result of triangular convergence of the Indian plate, the European plate and the Chinese plate.
    Which of these statements are correct? [47th B.P.S.C. (Pre) 2005]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer. Statement 1 is correct: The Meghalaya Plateau is an extension of the Deccan Plateau towards the east. It stretches from the Rajmahal Hills and is separated by the Garo-Rajmahal Gap. This gap was created by anormal fault, leading toa downward movement of a block of Earth. Sediments deposited by the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers later filled this gap. The plateau comprises Archaean quartzites, shales, schists and slopes towards the Brahmaputra valley in the north and the Surma and Meghna valleys in the south. Statement 2 is correct: A synclinorium is a type of fold where the layers of rock are bent downwards. The Kashmir Valley was formed when the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate. The collision caused the Earth’ crust to buckle and fold, creating the Pir Panjal and Zanskar ranges. The Kashmir Valley is located in the trough between these two mountain ranges. Statement 3 is correct: The Gangetic Plain, a vast alluvial plain in northern India, was created within a geological feature known as a foredeep. A foredeep is a depression created by the subsidence of the Earth’s crust adjacent to a mountain range. It formed as a result of the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate, with the Indian Plate sliding beneath the Eurasian Plate, causing the Eurasian Plate to push up and form the Himalayan Mountains while the foredeep region sank, accumulating sediments over millions of years, shaping the fertile Gangetic Plain. Statement 4 is incorrect: The Himalayas originated as a result of the collision of the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
Page 219

question: 1. Which one of the following can be used to make acidic soil cultivable? [M.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2006]

Calcium is a nutrient that is essential for plant growth,but it does not help to neutralize acidity. Vegetable compost is a good source of organic matter, but it does not have any alkaline propetties. Therefore, lime is the best option for making acidic soil cultivable.

Important Tips

  • Add organic matter to the soil. Organic matter helps to improve the soil structure and make it more alkaline.
  • Use a cover crop. A cover crop is a plant that is grown to cover the soil and prevent erosion. Cover crops also help to add organic matter to the soil.
  • Irrigate the soil regularly. Irrigation helps to flush out the acidic compounds from the soil.

question:
1. The dust storms originating in Rajasthan in May and June months are caused due to-
  2. Origin of convectional currents at few places
  3. Aravalli hills are parallel to south-western winds
  4. Origin of fast speedy easterly winds
    Code: [R.A.S/R.T.S. (Pre) 2018]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer. Statement 1 is correct- Dust storms that occur in Rajasthan during May and June are primarily driven by the formation of convectional currents at specific locations in the region. Convectional currents involve the circular movement of air due to temperature differences, with warmer, less dense air rising while cooler air descends. In Rajasthan, the intense heating of the desert air during the scorching summer months creates an unstable lower atmosphere, leading to the mixing of strong winds from the middle troposphere downward to the surface and resulting in stronger surface winds. These powerful winds, often associated with thunderstorms, give rise to dust storms. Statement 2 is incorrect- The Aravalli Mountain range runs parallel to the southwest monsoonwinds originating from the Arabian Sea. Consequently, these mountains do not effectively block these winds, resulting in western Rajasthan being characterized as a low-rainfall or arid region. Statement 3 is incorrect-Easterly Winds do not play a role in the origination of Dust Storms in Rajasthan. Easterly winds are generally weak and gentle winds, and they do not tend to create the strong, gusty winds that are necessary for dust storms to form. However, it helps to transport dust storms from Rajasthan to other parts of India.
Page 223

Lakshadweep consists of twelve atolls, three reefs, and five submerged banks, making ita region with numerous atolls. These atolls have a typical northeast-southwest orientation, with the islands located on the eastern rim and submerged reefs on the western rim, forming lagoons within. [Image: Diagrams of different types of coral reefs]

Important Tips

Different types of coral reef formations:

  • Fringing Reefs: These are coral reefs that develop in close proximity to the shore and extend outward into the sea, forming a submerged platform. For example, the Ningaloo Reef in Australia.
  • Barrier Reefs: Barrier reefs are located at a considerable distance from the shoreline, separated by wide expanses of water, and they run parallel to the coastline. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is a famous example.
  • Atolls: Atolls are circular formations of reefs that encircle a central lagoon, often surrounding a low-lying island. They are commonly found in the Indian and South Pacific Oceans, such as the Atolls of Lakshadweep.
  • Patch Reefs: These are small, isolated coral reefs that emerge from the open seabed of the continental shelf or island platform. They are typically situated between fringing reefs and barrier reefs, varying in size and rarely reaching the water’s surface.
    Page 225

question: 1. Which of the following rivers does not make estuary? [Jharkhand P.C.S. (Pre) 2003]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer. The Mahanadi River does not form an estuary. An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of brackish water formed where freshwater from rivers and streams meets and mixes with saltwater from the ocean or sea. The Narmada, Tapti, and Mandavi rivers do form estuaries as they meet the Arabian Sea. In the case of the Mahanadi River, it forms a delta as it empties into the Bay of Bengal. A delta is a landform created by the deposition of sediment carried by the river, typically resulting in a network of distributaries or channels as the river divides into smaller streams before reaching the sea.

Important Tips

Deltas are common in the East-flowing rivers of India, while they are nearly absent on the West coast:

  • Geological variation: East-flowing rivers pass through regions with broken hills and plateaus, promoting sediment—deposition. West-flowing tivers face steep, rocky Western Ghats, hampering sediment collection.
  • Velocity contrast: East-flowing rivers, with gentler gradients, have slower flows allowing sediment transport. West-flowing rivers maintain high speeds due to their steep gradients, impeding sediment accumulation.
  • Elevation difference: The eastward-sloping Deccan Plateau elevates the Western side, limiting low-lying areas for sediment deposition on the West coast.
  • Estuaries vs. Deltas: East-flowing rivers, with their ability to deposit sediments, often form deltas near their mouths. Deltas are characterized by their fan-like landforms created by the accumulation of sediments carried by the river. West-flowing rivers, due to their higher speeds and reduced sediment-carrying capacity, tend to form estuaries instead. Estuaries are transitional zones where freshwater meets seawater, but they lack the characteristic deltaic landforms.
    Page 226

question: 1. Koppen has used which of the following words for the climate of Great Plains of India? [Uttarakhand PCS (Pre) 2021]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. The Great Plains of India have a humid sub-tropical climate (Cwg) with dry winter. This climate type is characterized by hot summers, mild winters, and a pronounced monsoon season. The Great Plains of India cover the states of Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and parts of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.

Important Tips

Koppen climate classification system in India:
According to the Koppen climate classification system, India has six major climatic subtypes: Af (tropical wet), Am (tropical monsoon), Aw (tropical wet and dry), BSh (subtropical steppe), BWh (subtropical desert) and Cwa (humid subtropical). Some of the characteristics of these climatic subtypes are:

  • Af: This subtype is found in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep Islands and some parts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It has no dry season and receives abundant rainfall throughout the year. The average temperature of the coldest month is above 18°C.
  • Am: This subtype is found in most of the northeastern states, some parts of West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. It has a short dry season and a long monsoon season. The rainfall is very high and varies with the monsoon winds. The average temperature of the coldest month is above 18°C.
  • Aw: This subtype is found in most of the central and northern parts of India, including Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. It has a winter dry season and a summer wet season. The rainfall is moderate to low and depends on the summer monsoon. The average temperature of the coldest month is above 18°C.
  • BSh: This subtype is found in some parts of Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir. It is a semi-arid or dry climate with low rainfall and high evaporation. The summers are very hot, and the winters are mild to cool. The average temperature of the coldest month is above 18°C.
  • BWh: This subtype is found in some parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Ladakh. It is an arid or desert climate with very low rainfall and very high evaporation. The summers are extremely hot, and the winters are cold. The average temperature of the coldest month is below 18°C.
  • Cwa: This subtype is found in some parts of Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. It is a humid subtropical climate with a winter dry season and a summer wet season. The rainfall is high and varies with the monsoon winds. The summers are hot and humid, and the winters go from cool to cold. The average temperature of the coldest month is below 18°C but above -3°C.
    Page 227

question: 1. In which part of Uttarakhand are artesian wells found? [Uttarakhand P.C.S. (Mains) 2006]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. Artesian wells are found in the Tarai region of Uttarakhand. These flowing artesian wells are a unique feature of the Tarai zone, distinguished by their natural discharge of groundwater without the need for pumps. The Bhabar zone is characterized by porous and permeable sediments, forming the recharge area for the artesian aquifer system in the Tarai region. The elevation difference between the Bhabar zone and the Tarai zone creates the artesian head in the aquifer, allowing groundwater to naturally rise to the surface in the form of flowing wells. However, over-exploitation and environmental factors are causing a decline in the water flow from these wells, posing challenges for sustainable agricultural practices in the region.

Important Tips

Artesian Wells:

  • Artesian wells are groundwater sources characterized by natural flow without mechanical pumping.
  • They are typically found in confined aquifers, sandwiched between impermeable layers.
  • Water in artesian wells is under positive pressure, causing it to rise above the aquifer’s top.
  • These wells are prevalent in regions like the Tarai zone of Uttarakhand, India.
  • Water discharge in artesian wells is influenced by the elevation difference between the aquifer and the ground surface.
  • Overexploitation, deforestation, and climate change can impact artesian wells’ water flow.
  • Measures like installing control valves and conserving groundwater are essential to sustain these unique water sources.
    Page 229

question: 1. Identify the type of soil on the basis of given characteristics: 1. They contain a large proportion of sodium, potassium and magnesium, and thus, they are infertile. 2. Their structure ranges from sandy to loamy. 3. They are more widespread in western Gujarat, deltas of the eastern coast and in Sunderban areas of West Bengal. [CDS 2023 (II)]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer Soil is the most important renewable natural resource. It is the medium of plant growth and supports different types of living organisms on the earth. The soil is a living system. India has varied relief features, landforms, climatic realms and vegetation types. These have contributed to the development of various types of soils. Among these, saline soils are one of the major soil types found in the country. Saline soils contain high percentages of potassium, sodium, and magnesium. The presence of these salts makes the soil infertile and unsuitable for most crops. They can have a range of textures, including sandy and loamy, depending on the region and local conditions. Saline soils are commonly found in coastal regions, such as those in Gujarat, the deltas of the eastern coast, and the Sundarbans areas of West Bengal. These areas are influenced by the salinity of seawater, which contributes to the formation of saline soils.

Important Tips

  • Alluvial Soil: Found in the Indo-Gangetic plains, it is highly fertile and ideal for crops like rice, wheat, and sugarcane. It is rich in minerals and has a sandy to loamy texture.
  • Black Soil: Common in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, it is rich in iron and magnesium. It is moisture-retentive and perfect for cotton cultivation.
  • Red Soil: Found in regions like Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, it is slightly acidic and low in fertility but supports crops like pulses, millet, and oilseeds.
  • Laterite Soil: Found in high rainfall areas like Kerala and coastal Karnataka, it is rich in iron and aluminum but low in fertility, suitable for crops like tea, coffee, and cashews.
  • Peaty and Marshy Soil: Found in wetlands, it is rich in organic matter but acidic and poorly drained, suitable for rice and aquatic plants.
  • Arid Soil: Found in Rajasthan and Gujarat, it is sandy, dry, and low in fertility, supporting drought-resistant crops like millets and barley.
  • Forest Soil: Found in hilly areas like the Himalayas, it is rich in organic matter, supporting dense forests but not suitable for large-scale agriculture.
  • Desert Soil: Found in the Thar Desert, it is sandy, infertile, and prone to erosion, but irrigation allows the cultivation of crops like barley and wheat.
    Page 229, 230

question:
1. Consider the following characteristics of a soil type:
  2. These soils consist of various proportions of sand, silt and clay.
  3. These soils contain adequate proportions of potash, phosphoric acid and lime.
  4. These soils can be further classified on the basis of their age.
    Identify the type of soil on the basis of the given characteristics. [CDS-2023(I)]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer Alluvial soils are formed by the deposition of river sediments. They are typically found in floodplains and deltas. Alluvial soils are rich in nutrients, such as potash, phosphoric acid, and lime. They are also well-drained and easy to work with. Alluvial soils can be further classified on the basis of their age.

Important Tips

  • Black soil
  • Also known as regur soil, it is found in the Deccan Plateau and the valleys of the Narmada and Tapi rivers.
  • It is a very fertile soil, rich in organic matter, nitrogen, and phosphorus.
  • It is well-drained and has a high water holding capacity.
  • It is suitable for growing a variety of crops, including cotton, wheat, and millet.
  • Laterite soil
  • It is found in tropical and subtropical regions with high rainfall and high temperatures.
  • It is a reddish-brown soil that is rich in iron and aluminium.
  • It is not very fertile, as it is low in organic matter and nitrogen.
  • It is often used for growing crops that are tolerant of poor soil conditions, such as cashew nuts and rubber.
  • Arid soil
  • It is found in hot, dry regions with low rainfall.
  • It is a sandy or loamy soil that is low in organic matter and nutrients.
  • It is often used for grazing or for growing drought-resistant crops, such as wheat and barley.
    Page 231

Important Tips

Key findings ofIndian Forest survey report, 2021

  • The total forest and tree cover is 24.62% of the countrys geographical area, showing an increase of 0.28% compared to the previous assessment in 2019.
  • Forest cover increased by 0.22%, while **tree cover increased by 0.76%**at the national level.

  • The top five states with increased forest cover are Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Karnataka and Jharkhand.
  • Forest cover in hill districts decreased by 902 sq km (0.32%), while forest cover in tribal districts decreased by 655 sq km inside the RFA/GW and increased by 600 sq km outside.
  • The North-Eastern region experienced a decrease of 1,020 sq km (0.60%) in forest cover.
  • Mangrove cover increased by 0.34%.
  • The total carbon stock in forests increased by 79.4 million tonnes since 2019, reaching 7,204.0 million tonnes.
  • Approximately 22.27% of the forest cover is prone to forest fires.
  • Bamboo-bearing areas decreased by 10,594 sq km compared to the estimate in 2019.

  2. These are the lacustrine deposits of Pleistocene period. 2. These are found along the lower slopes of Pir Panjal.

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer Statement 1 is correct:Karewas are the thick deposits of glacial clay and other materials embedded with moraines. These are unconsolidated lacustrine deposits meaning they were formed in a lake. They were formed in Pleistocene period (1 Million years ago) when the entire Kashmir valley was under water. Statement 2 is correct:Due to the rise of Pir Panjal, the drainage was impounded and a lake of about 5000 sq. km area was developed, thus a basin was formed. Subsequently the lake was drained through Bramulla gorge. The deposits left in the process are known as Karewas. Statement 3 is correct: The fertile soil deposited by the ancient lakes in the Karewa formations is highly suitable for agriculture. The Kashmir Valley, with its Karewa deposits, is renowned for growing saffron, almonds, and walnuts.

  • The Arabian Sea branch of the Monsoon brings rain to the western part of Punjab because it blows from the Arabian Sea towards the Himalayas.As the winds rise up the Himalayas, they cool and condense, forming clouds. These clouds then release their moisture as rain on the western side of the Himalayas, including the state of Punjab.
  • The Bay of Bengal branch of the Monsoon brings rain to the eastern part of Punjab because it blows from the Bay of Bengal towards the Thar Desert.As the winds cross the Ganges Plain, they pick up moisture from the rivers and the soil. This moisture is then released as rain on the eastern side of the Himalayas, including the state of Punjab.

question: 1. Which one of the following with regard to Aridisol, one of the soil orders, is not correct? [CDS 2017 (I)]
options: Lack of water for plants during most part of the year
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. Aridisols are generally low in organic matter content. The arid conditions, combined with limited plant growth and decomposition, result in a scarcity of organic materials in the soil. Aridisol is a soil order that is typically found in arid or semi-arid regions characterized by limited rainfall and high evaporation rates. It is associated with desert-like conditions where water availability for plants is limited for most of the year.

Important Tips

Apart from Aridisols, there are several other soil orders, including:

  • Alfisols: Moderately weathered soils with a clay-rich subsurface horizon.
  • Andisols: Soils formed from volcanic ash or other volcanic materials.
  • Entisols: Recently formed soils with minimal development of horizons.
  • Gelisols: Soils that are permanently or seasonally frozen for significant portions of the year.
  • Histosols: Organic soils characterized by a high content of partially decomposed plant material (peat or muck).
  • Inceptisols: Young soils with only moderate development of horizons.
  • Mollisols: Soils with a dark, fertile surface horizon rich in organic matter.
  • Oxisols: Highly weathered tropical soils with a reddish color and low fertility.
  • Spodosols: Acidic forest soils with a subsurface accumulation of organic matter and aluminum and iron compounds.
  • Ultisols: Highly weathered soils with a clay-rich subsurface horizon and low natural fertility.

question:
1. What would be the influence on the weather conditions when in mid-winter a feeble high pressure develops over the North-Western part of India? 1. High and dry winds would blow outward from this high pressure area.
  2. The Northern plain would become cold. 3. Scorching winds (locally called loo) would blow during the day of time.
  3. There would be torrential rains brought by thunderstorms.
    Select the correct answer using the codes given below: [CDS 2014 (I)]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer. Statement 1 is correct: When a high-pressure system develops, it is characterized by sinking air. As the air sinks, it tends to spread outwards from the center of high pressure. This leads to the development of high and dry winds that blow away from the high-pressure area. These winds are typically dry because the sinking air suppresses the formation of clouds and precipitation. Statement 2 is correct: In the case of the North-Western part of India, when a feeble high-pressure system develops in mid-winter, it would bring colder air masses into the region. The sinking air associated with the high pressure prevents warm air from rising, leading to cooler temperatures in the Northern plain. Statement 3 is incorrect: Scorching winds, commonly known as “loo,” are hot and dry winds that typically occur in the summer months, particularly in the North-Western region of India. They are associated with the intense heating of the land, which creates a low-pressure system and draws in hot winds from the surrounding areas. Statement 4 is incorrect: High-pressure systems are generally associated with stable atmospheric conditions, where sinking air suppresses the formation of clouds and precipitation.

question:
1. Consider the following statements:
  2. The Great Northern Plains are formed by basins of three distinct river systems the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra.
  3. They are one of the most densely populated areas on Earth.
  4. Between the Yamuna at Delhi and the Bay of Bengal, nearly 1600 km away, there is a drop of only 200 metres in elevation.
    Which of the statements given above are correct? [CAPF 2023]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer
Statement 1 is correct: The Great Northern Plains are indeed formed by three distinct river systems — the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra rivers. These plains span across northern India and extend into parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. It is divided into three distinct parts: Indus Plains, Ganga Plains, and Brahmaputra Plains. The plains owe their formation to the gradational activities of these rivers and their tributaries, which have deposited fertile alluvial soil over time.
Statement 2 is correct: The Great Northern Plains are among the most densely populated regions in the world. The reasons for this include the fertile soil, availability of water from the river systems, and the favorable climate for agriculture, making the region ideal for human settlement and cultivation.
Statement 3 is correct: The plains have a very gentle slope from the Yamuna at Delhi to the Bay of Bengal, with a drop of only about 200 meters over a distance of approximately 1600 km. This gradual slope ensures the smooth flow of rivers, further aiding agricultural activities.

Important Tips

Area and Extent of Great Northern Plains:
The Great Plains cover an extensive area of approximately 700,000 square kilometers, spanning across northern India and neighboring regions.
Boundaries of Great Northern Plains:

  • Northern Boundary: Clearly marked by the Shiwalik Hills, which form the foothills of the Himalayas.
  • Southern Boundary: Wavy and irregular along the northern edge of Peninsular India
  • Western Boundary: Bordered by the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges, which lie in present-day Pakistan, marking the transition from the plains to more rugged terrain.
  • Eastern Boundary: Enclosed by the Purvanchal hills.

question: 1. Which one of the following statements about the Himalayas is not correct? [CAPF 2017]
options: Himalayan Frontal Faults (HFF) separates Himalaya from Tibet.
Indus and Sutlej rivers form antecedent drainage in Himalaya
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. The Himalayan Frontal Faults (HFF) do not separate Himalaya from Tibet, meaning that they are not the boundary between the two regions. The HFF are a series of reverse faults that demarcate the boundary of the Siwalik Range, which is the southernmost range of the Himalayas, from the alluvial expanse of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, which is a large plain in northern India and Pakistan. The HFF are also known as the Main Frontal Thrust or the Himalayan Frontal Thrust.

Important Tips

  • The Himalayas are young fold mountains, meaning that they are formed by the folding and uplifting of the Earth’s crust due to tectonic forces.
  • The Himalayas have geosynclinal rocks, meaning that they have rocks that were deposited in a geosyncline, whichis a long and narrow trough of sedimentary rock between two tectonic plates
  • The Indus and Sutlej rivers form antecedent drainage in Himalaya, meaning that they have maintained their courses across the rising mountain ranges. Antecedent drainage is a type of drainage pattern in which a river or stream cuts through a mountain barrier that is uplifted due to tectonic forces.

question: 1. Which one among the following is the most plausible explanation for the location of the Thar Desert in Western India?[CAPF 2014]
options: The absence of mountains to the North of Rajasthan to cause orographic rainfall in it.
The Moisture carried by the South-West Monsoon is driven away by the dry upper at current.
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer. The most plausible explanation for the location of the Thar Desert in Western India is the absenceof mountains to the north of Rajasthan that could cause orographic rainfall in the region. Unlike other areas where mountains can trigger rainfall by forcing moist air to rise, the Thar Desert lacks significant mountain ranges in its northern vicinity. The Aravalli Range in southern Rajasthan acts as a barrier, preventing moisture-laden winds from the Arabian Sea from reaching the northern parts of the region. As a result, the area experiences arid or semi-arid conditions, leading to the formation of the Thar Desert. [Image: Diagram showing types of rainfall]

Important Tips

Different types of rainfall in India:

  • Convectional rainfall: It is caused by the sun heating the ground, which causes the air above it to warm up and rise. As the air rises, it cools and condenses, forming clouds. When the water droplets in the clouds become too large, they fall as rain. Convectional rainfall is common in tropical regions, where the sun is strong, and the air is warm.
  • Frontal rainfall: It is caused by the meeting of two air masses with different temperatures and humidities. When the air masses meet, they force each other up, which causes the air to cool and condense. When the water droplets in the clouds become too large, they fall as rain. Frontal rainfall is common in temperate regions, where the weather is more variable.

question:
1. Consider the following statements:
    Statement I: Some rare earth elements are used in the manufacture of flat television, screens and computer monitors.
    Statement II: Some rare earth elements have phosphorescent properties.
    Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.

Rare earth elements (REEs) are a group of 17 chemically similar elements, including the 15 lanthanides along with scandium and yttrium. These elements possess unique magnetic , luminescent, and electrochemical properties , making them essential in various high-tech applications, including electronics, renewable energy, and defense.

Statement I is correct . Rare earth elements such as **europium, terbium, and yttrium are integral in the production of phosphors used in display technologies **. These phosphors emit specific colours when excited by electrons, enabling the vivid displays in flat-screen televisions and computer monitors. For instance, europium is used for red phosphors, terbium for green, and yttrium serves as a host lattice for these phosphors .

Statement II is correct . Certain rare earth elements exhibit phosphorescence, a type of photoluminescence where materials emit light after being energized. Elements like europium and terbium are known for their phosphorescent properties , which are harnessed in various applications, including lighting and display technologies.

Statement II explains Statement I. The **phosphorescent properties of rare earth elements are the reason they are used in manufacturing display screens **. The ability of these elements to emit light upon excitation is fundamental to the functioning of phosphors in screens, thereby directly linking their phosphorescent nature to their application in display technologies.

Ilmenite (FeTiO3 ) and rutile (TiO2) are both minerals that contain high concentrations of **titanium **. Titanium is a strong and lightweight metal known for its excellent corrosion resistance and high strength-to-weight ratio. It is widely used in various industries , including aerospace, automotive, medical , and construction.

In India , certain coastal tracts are known for their significant **ilmenite and rutile deposits **. These minerals are commonly found in beach sand deposits and are extracted through beach sand mining operations. The extracted ilmenite and rutile are processed to obtain titanium dioxide (TiO2), which is then further refined to produce metallic titanium. Therefore, ilmenite and rutile, found abundantly in certain coastal tracts of India, are valuable sources of titanium.

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer

The DRC (The Democratic Republic of the Congo) is the world’s largest producer of cobalt, accounting for about three-fourths (75%) of the global production. The country has been the top producer of the metal for some time, and reported output of 130,000 MT in 2022. Cobalt is a crucial component in the manufacture of batteries for electric vehicles , as well as for various electronic devices such as smartphones and laptops .

There are several reasons why the DRC has become the primary source of cobalt production:

  • Abundance of Cobalt Reserves: The DRC is home to vast reserves of cobalt . It is estimated to have approximately 3.4 million metric tons of cobalt reserves, which is the largest in the world . This abundance of cobalt resources has made the DRC a significant player in the global cobalt market.
  • Artisanal Mining: A significant portion of cobalt production in the DRC comes from artisanal and small-scale mining operations. These operations involve individual miners or small groups extracting cobalt using basic tools and equipment. However, due to the informal nature of this mining sector , it can be associated with challenges such as poor working conditions, environmental concerns, and potential human rights issues.
  • Industrial Mining Operations: Alongside artisanal mining , the DRC also has large-scale industrial mining operations run by multinational mining companies. These operations use modern machinery and technologies to extract cobalt from mines. The industrial mining sector plays a crucial role in meeting the global demand for cobalt .

1. Consider the following statements:
    Assertion (A): There are no tea plantations in any African country.
    Reason (R ): Tea Plants need fertile soil with high humus .
    Code:
options: Both (A) and (R ) are individually true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A ) and (R) are individually true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.

Assertion (A ) is false because there are many tea plantations in several African countries , such as Kenya, Uganda , Tanzania, Malawi, South Africa , and Zambia. Kenya is the highest producer of tea in Africa and the third-largest producer in the world. Tea is one of the major export crops and sources of income for many African countries.

Reason (R) is true because tea plants do need fertile soil with high humus content . Humus is the organic matter that improves the soil structure, water retention , nutrient availability, and microbial activity. Tea plants also prefer acidic soil with a pH between 4 .5 and 5.5, and a medium to high level of organic matter . However, this is not the reason why there are no tea plantations in some African countries , as there are other factors such as climate , rainfall, elevation, pests, diseases , and market demand that affect tea production.

Important Tips

Some of the conditions for tea plantation are:

  • Temperature: Tea plants prefer cool to warm temperatures, with a mean annual temperature of 18 °C to 21°C during the growing season.
  • Rainfall : Tea plants need heavy rainfall, ranging from 150 cm to 250 cm per year, with a well-distributed pattern throughout the year.
  • Humidity: Tea plants thrive in high humidity , with a relative humidity of 70% to 90 % during the growing season .
  • Soil: Tea plants require fertile soil with high humus content and good drainage.
  • Altitude: Tea plants can grow from sea level to high altitudes , but the quality and flavor of tea vary depending on the elevation .

options: Both (A) and (R ) are correct, and (R ) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A ) and (R) are correct , but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.

Assertion (A ) is true: Gondwana system of rocks contains nearly 98% of India’s coal reserves. The Gondwana system is also called the Carboniferous system because it was formed during the Carboniferous period, about 300 million years ago. The Gondwana rocks are mainly composed of sandstones, shales , and coal seams that were deposited in large basins by rivers and lakes.

Reason (R) is correct but do not correctly explain Assertion (A): The Dharwar system of rocks is a highly metamorphosed sedimentary rock system that formed between 2.5 billion to 1.8 billion years ago . The Dharwar rocks are mainly schists, phyllites, and slates that contain valuable minerals like iron ore , manganese, copper, lead, gold , etc.

Important Tips

Coal Formation:
Coal is a sedimentary rock that forms from the accumulation and compression of plant matter over millions of years . The Gondwana System of Rocks dates back to the Carboniferous and Permian periods, when most of the landmasses were united in a supercontinent called Gondwana. During this time , vast swamps and forests covered the land, providing abundant organic material for coal formation.

question: 1. The most mineralized rock system of India is-
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.

The most mineralized rock system of India is the Dharwar System. This system is composed of highly metamorphosed sedimentary rocks that are rich in valuable minerals like high grade iron-ore , manganese, copper, lead, gold , etc. The Dharwar System is found in abundance in the Dharwar district of Karnataka and also in some parts of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh , Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan .

Important Tips

Rock system of India:

  • Cuddapah System: This system consists of sedimentary rocks that are mainly composed of quartzites, shales , limestones and dolomites. The Cuddapah System is found in the Cuddapah basin of Andhra Pradesh and also in some parts of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Chhattisgarh. The Cuddapah System is not very rich in minerals, but it contains some deposits of barite, asbestos, corundum , steatite, etc.
  • Gondwana System: This system comprises of sedimentary rocks that were formed during the Carboniferous to Jurassic periods. The Gondwana System is widely distributed in the peninsular India , especially in the Damodar , Mahanadi, Godavari and Narmada valleys. The Gondwana System is known for its coal deposits, which are the main source of energy in India. The Gondwana System also contains some other minerals like iron-ore, copper, uranium, etc.
  • Vindhyan System: This system consists of sedimentary rocks that are mainly composed of sandstones, shales and limestones . The Vindhyan System is found in the Vindhyan basin of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh and also in some parts of Rajasthan, Bihar and Jharkhand. The Vindhyan System is poor in mineral resources, but it has some deposits of glass sand, potash, rock phosphate , etc.

A . Iron ore is a metal that is used to make steel and other products. It is found in many places around the world, but one of the largest and most famous iron ore deposits is the **Mesabi Range in Minnesota, USA **. The Mesabi Range has been mined since the late 19th century and has produced over 3 billion tons of iron ore.

B. Petroleum is a liquid fossil fuel that is used for energy , transportation, and manufacturing. It is formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals that were buried under layers of sediment and subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years. Petroleum is extracted from underground reservoirs or wells, and one of the oldest and most prolific oil-producing regions is Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan. Baku lies on the Caspian Sea and has been producing oil since the 7th century BC. It was the world’s first oil boomtown in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when it supplied half of the world’s oil.

C. Copper is a metal that is used for electrical wiring , plumbing, coins, and other purposes. It is found in various types of ore deposits, such as porphyry, skarn, hydrothermal, and sedimentary. One of the largest and most impressive copper mines in the world is Bingham Canyon Mine in Utah, USA. Bingham Canyon Mine is an open pit mine that has been operating since 1906 and has produced more than 19 million tons of copper. It is also the largest man-made excavation and the deepest open pit mine in the world.

question: 1. Which of the following soil formation process takes place in Phumdis (floating fields) in Loktak Lake of Manipur?
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer

**Phumdis ** are floating islands made of a heterogeneous mixture of vegetation, soil, and organic matter at different stages of decomposition. These floating fields are unique to Loktak Lake in Manipur. The soil formation process in Phumdis involves Gleization, which occurs in waterlogged or poorly drained areas .

Important Tips

  • Gleization is a soil formation process that takes place under waterlogged conditions. It occurs in areas where drainage is poor, leading to the accumulation of water and the creation of anaerobic (oxygen-deprived) conditions. The reduced decomposition leads to the accumulation of organic matter , similar to what is observed in the Phumdis of Loktak Lake. In Gleization, iron compounds in the soil are reduced due to the anaerobic environment , and this gives the soil a gray or bluish color, typical in wetland areas.
  • Laterization: This is a process associated with the formation of laterite soils in hot and humid climates, where leaching occurs, leading to the concentration of iron and aluminum oxides.
  • Podzolization: This process occurs in cold, humid environments, typically under coniferous forests, and leads to the formation of acidic soils with a leached , sandy upper layer.
  • Calcification : Calcification is the process of calcium carbonate accumulation in soils, typical of dry or semi-arid regions .

1. Which of the following are the necessary conditions for the growth of coral reefs?
  2. Photic conditions
  3. Clean and sediment-free water
  4. Sea salinity of 6%
    4 . Tropical Sea water with temperature of 20°C - 21 °C
    Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.

Coral reefs are underwater structures made of calcium carbonate secreted by corals, which are marine animals that live in symbiosis with algae called zooxanthellae. The necessary conditions for the growth of coral reefs are:

  • Photic conditions: Corals need to grow in shallow water where sunlight can reach them. Sunlight is essential for the photosynthesis of the zooxanthellae , which provide nutrients and oxygen to the corals.
  • Clean and sediment-free water: Corals need clear water that lets sunlight through. Sediment and pollution can reduce the light penetration, smother the corals, and interfere with their feeding and reproduction.
  • Sea salinity of 6%: This is **not ** a necessary condition for the growth of coral reefs. Sea salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in seawater, which is usually around 3 .5%. Corals can tolerate a range of salinity levels, but they prefer stable conditions.
  • Tropical sea water with temperature of 20°C - 21°C: This is a necessary condition for the growth of coral reefs. Most corals are found in tropical and subtropical regions, where the water temperature is between 20°C and 32°C.
    Page 297

question: 1. How can resources be classified on the basis of their origin ?
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer

Option a is correct: Resources can be classified based on their origin into biotic and abiotic resources. Biotic resources are those that come from living organisms such as such as human beings, flora and fauna, fisheries, livestock etc . whereas abiotic resources are inorganic components derived from the non-living organisms such as water, air, minerals , rocks and metals.

Option b is incorrect: Renewable and non-renewable classify resources based on their **exhaustibility **. Renewable resources are those which get renewed or replenished quickly. Non-renewable resources are those which have a limited stock. Once the stocks are exhausted it may take thousands of years to be renewed or replenished.

Option c is incorrect: Individual and community classify resources based on ownership. Individual resources are resources owned by individuals whereas community resources are shared among a community or group.

Option d is incorrect: Potential and reserve classify resources based on their **current availability and potential future use **. Potential resources are resources that exist in a region and could be used in the future but are not currently being exploited whereas reserve resources are a part of the known resources that are currently available for use.

By displaying both age-groups and sex indicators, population pyramids provide a comprehensive overview of the age and sex composition of a population, facilitating the analysis of demographic trends and patterns.

Important Tips

Population Pyramid:

  • A population pyramid , also known as an age-sex pyramid, is a graphical illustration of the distribution of a population (typically that of a country or region of the world) by age groups and sex.
  • It typically takes the shape of a pyramid when the population is growing . The population pyramid is divided into two halves , with the male population on the left and the female population on the right.
  • The age groups are typically divided into five-year intervals, starting with the youngest age group at the bottom and the oldest age group at the top .
  • The width of each bar in the population pyramid represents the number of people in that age group and sex . The height of the pyramid represents the total population.
  • A population pyramid with a broad base and a narrow top indicates a growing population , while a population pyramid with a narrow base and a broad top indicates a declining population .

  5. Low death rate and birthrate, low growth rate.

explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.

Statement 1 is correct: High death rate and birthrate , low growth rate describes the initial stage of demographic transition when both birth rates and death rates are high, resulting in a relatively low growth rate.
Statement 4 is correct: Low death rate and birthrate, low growth rate describes the fourth and final stage of demographic transition. In this stage, both the death rate and birth rate are low, resulting in a low growth rate or even population decline .

Important Tips

  • Demographic transition (DT) refers to the transition from high birth and death rates to lower birth and death rates as a country or region develops from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economic system .
  • The theory was proposed in **1929 by the American demographer Warren Thompson **, who observed changes, or transitions, in birth and death rates in industrialized societies over the previous 200 years.
  • Most developed countries have completed the demographic transition and have low birth rates; most developing countries are in the process of this transition.
